quote: Wenn am Schluss einer Debatte mehrere Anträge vorliegen (etwa $n=3$ Anträge) wie soll abgestimmt werden.
english: If at the end of a debate several motions are pending (say n=3 motions), how should the vote be conducted?
topic: Hilbert argues that the axiomatic method is indispensable in set theory, resolving the paradox of the set of all sets by denying that it is a consistent axiomatically definable set, and then considers how to order the voting when several motions are pending at the end of a debate, listing the 8 possible outcomes for 3 motions.

triage.modern_statement: This is a question about how to design a voting procedure. n binary motions are pending, giving 2^n possible joint outcomes (8 when n=3). The question is how to order and structure the votes (motion-by-motion votes, sequential or amendment agendas, or one vote over all 2^n combinations) so that the collective result faithfully reflects the voters' preferences. In modern terms this belongs to social choice theory. Specifically it concerns order-of-voting (agenda) effects under the amendment and successive procedures, and combinatorial voting on multiple binary issues, where separate issue-by-issue majority votes may yield a combination that no voter actually supports. Hilbert's note poses the question but gives no precise conjecture, so it is a loose design question rather than a sharp theorem.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert did not answer it himself, and it is not one of his 23 problems or the 24th problem. The broader question was taken up later in social choice theory. Duncan Black and Robin Farquharson (Farquharson's work dates to 1957/1969) analysed order-of-voting effects and sophisticated (strategic) voting under amendment and successive agendas. Kenneth Arrow (Social Choice and Individual Values, 1951) showed that no ranked voting rule over 3 or more alternatives satisfies all of a set of reasonable conditions. Brams, Kilgour and Zwicker (Social Choice and Welfare, 1998) studied the exact setting of yes/no votes on three propositions and identified the 'paradox of multiple elections'. These works do not give a single best procedure. They settle the question negatively: the result can depend on the voting order, and no procedure is ideal.

evidence.claim: Brams, Kilgour and Zwicker study voters choosing yes or no on three propositions in a referendum. The winning combination can differ from every ballot actually submitted (the paradox of multiple elections).
Brams, Kilgour and Zwicker (1998) are cited as showing that the final set of approved outcomes may not match any single ballot. Ahn's later combinatorial-voting paper builds on this.
Black and Farquharson's results on order-of-voting effects under the amendment and successive procedures are extended using algorithms for computing sincere and sophisticated outcomes.
Sophisticated agenda voting (Farquharson 1957/1969) is used to study which majority voting rules can be implemented.
Arrow's impossibility theorem appeared in his 1951 book Social Choice and Individual Values. It is a central result of social choice theory.

triage.why: The note fits a well-known area: voting on several pending motions, the 2^n outcome combinations, and the order of votes. That area later became formal social choice theory, through agenda and order-of-voting effects (Black, Farquharson), Arrow's theorem, and combinatorial voting (Brams-Kilgour-Zwicker 1998, Ahn and others). Research continues on agenda implementation and combinatorial or multi-issue voting. My search found no source showing that Hilbert's note influenced any of this work, and it is not among his published problems. Because the note is informal, it cannot be tied to one specific theorem. 'Solved' here means the question was thoroughly analysed later, not that it has one definitive answer.
